items.readable_text:
Content:
The angle-side-angle (ASA) congruence criterion can be used as a shortcut to prove that two triangles are congruent. It states the following:

Content:
> Two triangles are congruent if and only if two angles and the included side of one triangle are congruent to two angles and the included side of the other triangle.

Content:
To demonstrate, consider the triangles below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/bc5bddd9139cecb03b195f0382044346]

Content:
We can see that two pairs of angles are congruent:

Content:
[MATH: \angle{A}\cong \angle{K}, \quad
\angle{B}\cong \angle{L} \quad]

Content:
Also, we see that the included sides are congruent:

Content:
[MATH: \overline{AB}\cong \overline{KL}]

Content:
Therefore, the ASA congruence criterion guarantees that these two triangles are congruent, and we can write

Content:
[MATH: \triangle ABC \cong \triangle KLM.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The ASA (angle-side-angle) congruence criterion states the following:

Two triangles are congruent if and only if two angles and the included side of one triangle are congruent to two angles and the included side of the other triangle.

With that in mind, let's examine each of the given triangles.

  • [MATH: \mathcal{P}] is not congruent to [MATH: \mathcal{T}_1] by ASA since they don't have congruent angles.

  • [MATH: \mathcal{P}] is not congruent to [MATH: \mathcal{T}_2] by ASA since they don't have congruent sides.

  • [MATH: \mathcal{P} \cong \mathcal{T}_3] by ASA since two angles and the included side of one triangle are congruent to two angles and the included side of the other triangle.

Therefore, only [MATH: \mathcal{T}_3] is congruent to [MATH: \mathcal{P}] by the ASA criterion.

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The angle-side-angle (ASA) congruence criterion can be used as a shortcut to prove that two triangles are congruent. It states the following:

Content:
> Two triangles are congruent if and only if two angles and the included side of one triangle are congruent to two angles and the included side of the other triangle.

Content:
To demonstrate, consider the triangles below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/bc5bddd9139cecb03b195f0382044346]

Content:
We can see that two pairs of angles are congruent:

Content:
[MATH: \angle{A}\cong \angle{K}, \quad
\angle{B}\cong \angle{L} \quad]

Content:
Also, we see that the included sides are congruent:

Content:
[MATH: \overline{AB}\cong \overline{KL}]

Content:
Therefore, the ASA congruence criterion guarantees that these two triangles are congruent, and we can write

Content:
[MATH: \triangle ABC \cong \triangle KLM.]

---

With that in mind, let's examine each of the given triangles.

- [MATH: \mathcal{P}] is not congruent to [MATH: \mathcal{T}_1] by ASA since they don't have congruent angles.
- [MATH: \mathcal{P}] is not congruent to [MATH: \mathcal{T}_2] by ASA since they don't have congruent sides.
